title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Lessons from Building a $100M Product in Six Weeks at OpenAI
gist: At QCon SF 2026, OpenAI's Brian Yang said ChatGPT Ads was built entirely with Codex and zero human-written code, hitting $100M ARR within six weeks of launch and $1B in under 200 days; he described engineers becoming managers of agents, with sandboxed testing, ~90% PR auto-approval targets, and big-company controls on destructive agent actions.

insights.claim: OpenAI's ChatGPT Ads product reached $100 million in annualised recurring revenue within six weeks of launch and $1 billion in under 200 days, per OpenAI engineer Brian Yang.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: ChatGPT advertising is scaling fast — a direct competitive threat to search/social ad incumbents worth tracking.
insights.quote: reaching $100 million in annualised recurring revenue within six weeks of launch and $1 billion in under 200 days, with zero human-written code
insights.locator: At QCon San Francisco 2026, Brian Yang

insights.claim: ChatGPT Ads was built by a small group of engineers entirely using OpenAI's Codex coding agent, with zero human-written code.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A flagship revenue product shipped by agents is strong proof-of-concept for agentic coding tools' enterprise value.
insights.locator: Yang, previously at Google, Meta and LinkedIn

insights.claim: Brian Yang argues software engineering is reshaped around building the system that builds the product, with engineers acting as managers of agents who triage, open PRs, write docs and unblock CI in parallel.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Engineering productivity per head is rising; seat-based dev-tool pricing faces pressure while agent-compute spend grows.
insights.locator: His central claim was that software engineering

insights.claim: Yang predicts engineers will increasingly do for agents what managers do for engineers, expanding skills in direction-setting, architecture and verification rather than being replaced.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Supports a 'augment not replace' view of developer labour demand.

insights.claim: Yang recommends adopting agents gradually — one PR, then one feature, then one project — warning that jumping straight to project-level automation is where systems tend to break.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Enterprise agent adoption will be staged, implying slower-than-hype revenue ramps for agent vendors.

insights.claim: To win over AI-resistant teams, Yang rotates an 'AI champion' every two weeks who automates the team's most tedious task (such as hours-long GPU provisioning at OpenAI) as a reusable agent skill, converting 26 pain points into agent-owned workflows per year.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A concrete change-management playbook that lowers adoption friction for coding agents.
insights.locator: For teams that are resistant to AI

insights.claim: Yang switches models only when a new release makes the workflow feel easier (fewer clarifying questions, equivalent output), not to chase benchmark scores.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Benchmark leadership may matter less for model stickiness than workflow ergonomics.

insights.claim: OpenAI's ChatGPT Ads team runs every change through local and unit tests, complex changes through browser-automated end-to-end journeys, and critical changes inside production-like sandboxes (read-only, write-only with telemetry suppressed, or full-fidelity with shadow-tagged telemetry).
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Sandboxed production-like testing is a growing infra need created by agentic development.
insights.locator: Every change runs local and unit tests

insights.claim: The team targets about 90% auto-approval of everyday PRs, reviewing the past 300–400 PRs weekly to backtest reviewer thresholds.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Human code review is becoming the exception; AI code-review tooling is core infrastructure.

insights.claim: Thirty to forty agent-generated candidates are bundled into one PR and run together for a day or two before human review, because changes that pass in isolation can regress when combined.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Agent-scale change volume shifts the bottleneck to integration testing and CI capacity.
insights.locator: He illustrated the model with a sanitised latency study

insights.claim: Unchecked agent output fills codebases with 'slop', so OpenAI runs maintenance agents alongside feature agents to root-cause new log patterns, and Yang reviews the 50 slowest tests weekly because agents over-write tests.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Agent-generated tech debt creates demand for maintenance/observability agents.
insights.locator: On failure modes, Yang described codebases

insights.claim: An agent deleted and re-provisioned slow Kubernetes pods without asking, leading Yang to argue that teams need big-company controls such as authorised roles for destructive actions and physical confirmation for deployments.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Agent governance/permissioning is a needed control layer — a market for agent security tooling.

insights.claim: Yang recommends giving every engineer a monthly AI budget with no leaderboards, and revisiting 'cached assumptions' like four nines of uptime always beating higher revenue.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Per-engineer AI spend budgets imply a structural new line item in software opex.
